**Title:** Survival Outcomes in Metastatic Colorectal Cancer Patients with BRAF Mutations Undergoing Targeted Chemotherapy: A Reconstructed Individual Patient Data Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.

**Authors:** Syeda Kanza Kazmi, Muhammad Abdul Rehman, Hanaa Tariq, Aqsa Kabir, Jalib Ahmed, Nelson Shu-Sang S Yee

**Journal:** Journal of gastrointestinal cancer
**Publication Date:** 2026-10-30
**DOI:** 10.1007/s12029-026-01597-6
**PMC ID:** 13719800
**Full Text Available:** Yes
**Full Text URL:** https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC13719800/


**Abstract:**
BRAF V600E-mutant metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC) represents an aggressive molecular subtype associated with poor prognosis and limited response to conventional chemotherapy. Although multiple targeted strategies, including anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), anti-epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), and BRAF-directed therapies, are used in clinical practice, their comparative effectiveness remains uncertain. We performed a reconstructed individual patient-data (IPD) meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) to evaluate survival outcomes across targeted therapeutic classes in BRAF-mutant mCRC.

BRAF V600E–mutant metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC) represents an aggressive molecular subtype associated with poor prognosis and limited response to conventional chemotherapy. Although multiple targeted strategies, including anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), anti-epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), and BRAF-directed therapies, are used in clinical practice, their comparative effectiveness remains uncertain. We performed a reconstructed individual patient–data (IPD) meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) to evaluate survival outcomes across targeted therapeutic classes in BRAF-mutant mCRC.

A systematic search of PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Cochrane databases was conducted through July 2025 to identify RCTs reporting survival outcomes for BRAF-mutant mCRC. Kaplan–Meier curves were digitized and IPD reconstructed using established methods. A one-stage meta-analysis using Cox proportional hazards models was performed to estimate pooled overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS). Models were adjusted for study-level covariates and clustering, with Bonferroni correction applied for multiple comparisons.

Eighteen RCTs comprising 11,931 participants were included. Pooled median OS was 22.3 months for BRAF-directed regimens, 17.1 months for VEGF-targeted therapy, and 10.1 months for EGFR-directed therapy across studies evaluating first-line therapy. Across first-line studies, BRAF inhibitor directed regimen was associated with significantly improved OS compared with EGFR inhibition (HR 0.43, 95% CI 0.31–0.60; P < 0.001) and improved PFS (HR 0.47, 95% CI 0.42–0.53; P < 0.001). VEGF inhibition also demonstrated superior OS compared with EGFR inhibition (HR 0.56, 95% CI 0.38–0.81; p < 0.001). EGFR-directed regimen consistently demonstrated the poorest survival outcomes across analyses.

In this reconstructed IPD meta-analysis, BRAF-directed therapies were associated with the most favourable survival outcomes, whereas EGFR directed regimen demonstrated limited clinical benefit in BRAF-mutant mCRC. These results highlight the importance of biologically aligned pathway-targeted therapy and provide comparative evidence to inform treatment selection in this aggressive molecular subtype.

The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s12029-026-01597-6.

Keywords: BRAF V600E mutation, Metastatic colorectal cancer, Targeted Therapy, Anti-EGFR, anti-VEGF, meta-analysis

Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the third most common cancer worldwide and the second leading cause of cancer-mortality in the world [1]. The American Cancer Society projected an estimated 52,900 deaths due to CRC in 2025 [2]. Despite advancement in screening and treatment, metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC) accounts for the majority of CRC-related deaths [3], with a 5-year survival rate of 16.2% [2].

mCRC is a heterogeneous malignancy characterised by various molecular subtypes. BRAF-mutated mCRC is seen in 8–10% of patients with mCRC [4]. Among these, BRAF V600E mutation, which constitutes > 90% of BRAF-mutant malignancies, represents a distinctly aggressive phenotype associated with poorer overall prognosis and worse response to standard chemotherapy [4, 5]. While historically mCRC treatment has largely been based on combination irinotecan or oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy regimens [6], over the past several years it has become increasingly clear that molecular-targeted therapies play a pivotal role in mCRC management. The National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) currently recommends testing for BRAF status, as well as KRAS/NRAS status, in mCRC patients in order to guide treatment [7].

The management of BRAF V600E-mutant mCRC remains a formidable challenge for oncologists, with a complex treatment landscape that has evolved rapidly over the past several years [8]. The anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) agent bevacizumab, in combination with doublet or triplet chemotherapy, has historically been recommended as standard of care for first-line treatment of BRAF-mutant mCRC [7, 9]. This was supported by evidence from studies such as a phase II trial which demonstrated an increase in 6-month progression-free rate for BRAF V600E-mutant patients treated with FOLFOXIRI (folinic acid, fluorouracil, oxaliplatin, and irinotecan) combined with bevacizumab [10]. The prospective, randomized FIRE-4.5 trial also reinforced the superiority of bevacizumab-based chemotherapy compared to chemotherapy with the anti-epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) agent cetuximab for BRAF V600E-mutant mCRC [11].

Conversely, while anti-EGFR agents such as cetuximab or panitumumab are often used in combination with chemotherapy for RAS-wild type (wt) and BRAF-wt mCRC, their role in the treatment of BRAF-mutated mCRC has remained controversial [9]. Evidence has increasingly pointed towards BRAF mutation being a negative predictive marker for response to anti-EGFR therapy alone or in combination with chemotherapy [12, 13]. Similarly, BRAF inhibitors, when used alone, have not been shown to confer a significant benefit in the treatment of BRAF-mutant mCRC [14]. These findings highlight the complex nature of the MAPK signalling pathway and resistance mechanisms in this disease.

However, the treatment landscape shifted significantly after the results of the BEACON CRC study, which established the role of anti-EGFR therapy, along with the BRAF inhibitor encorafenib, as the standard of care for previously treated BRAF-mutant mCRC. The results of this trial demonstrated improvement in overall survival (OS), progression-free survival (PFS) and overall response rate (ORR), compared to standard chemotherapy regimens [15]. Building on these findings, the recent BREAKWATER trial showed significantly improved OS and PFS with encorafenib plus cetuximab and chemotherapy, compared to standard of care for previously untreated BRAF V600E-mutant mCRC as well [16]. Based on this evidence, new guidelines now recommend this regimen for first-line treatment of BRAF-mutant mCRC [17].

When taken together, these observations highlight that the management of BRAF V600E-mutant mCRC remains a moving target. While newer trials have enhanced treatment options, the choice of therapeutic strategy has become more complex, with the comparative effectiveness of these therapies remaining unclear. Furthermore, existing data largely relies on post-hoc subgroup analyses and small sample sizes, limiting the ability to draw meaningful comparative conclusions. Therefore, this reconstructed individual patient-data (IPD) meta-analysis was designed in order to enhance statistical power by pooling reconstructed individual patient data across randomized control trials (RCTs) and thereby increase sample size. In doing so, we aim to provide a more comprehensive analysis of survival outcomes in BRAF-mutant mCRC to further guide optimal evidence-based management.

This review is reported as per the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-Analyses of individual participant data (PRISMA-IPD) reporting guidelines [18]. The PRISMA flowchart is shown in Fig. 1.

To be eligible for this review, only RCTs evaluating targeted therapy for mCRC patients were considered. Trials had to report survival data for BRAF-mutated mCRC through at least one Kaplan-Meier curve and also provide the starting number at risk. Study designs other than RCTs, trials which did not evaluate targeted therapy, did not evaluate mCRC patients, or did not report at least one Kaplan-Meier curve were excluded.

In July 2025, we searched PubMed, Scopus, Embase, and Cochrane using major keywords “BRAF”, “metastatic colorectal cancer”, and “survival”. We did not limit our search to any particular year. Complete search strings for each individual database are present in the Supplementary File.

Articles found during the initial search were moved to Rayyan and then de-duplicated. Next, the articles were divided between two teams of two authors, each. Each team independently screened articles based on titles and abstracts. Short-listed articles were then reviewed by reading the full manuscript using a similar approach. At any stage, if the two authors disagreed on the eligibility of an article, a third author, outside the team, was consulted who made the final decision.

For eligible studies, we extracted data onto a pre-defined template. Data was independently extracted by AT, HT, and SKK. Any discrepancies were resolved independently by a third author.

Survival data for IPD was reconstructed using Kaplan-Meier curves in eligible studies. Kaplan-Meier curves were digitized via WebPlotDigitizer and redrawn [19]. Coordinates were converted to survival times and event indicators using established methods. Reconstructed curves were visually inspected and also verified numerically by comparing reconstructed median survival times against original values as shown in Supplementary Fig. 1.

Treatment arms were classified into therapeutic classes based on the primary targeted mechanism of action. ‘BRAF-directed regimens’ included any arm in which a BRAF inhibitor constituted the principal targeted agent, regardless of whether anti-EGFR therapy or chemotherapy was co-administered. ‘EGFR-directed regimens’ included arms using anti-EGFR agents without concurrent BRAF inhibition. ‘VEGF-directed regimens’ included arms using anti-VEGF agents as the primary targeted therapy.

We assessed risk of bias amongst included studies using the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool for randomized trials version 2 (RoB 2) [20].This tool evaluates five domains: randomization, deviations from intended interventions, missing outcome data, outcome measurement, and selection of reported results. Each domain is rated as either ‘low risk’, ‘some concerns’, or ‘high risk’. Risk of bias was independently performed by HT.

We conducted a one-stage meta-analysis to pool IPD data from eligible studies. Time-to-event was reconciled in months. We assessed proportionality by visually assessing Shoenfield’s residuals. If the assumption was not violated, we fit a proportional hazards Cox model. If the assumption was violated, we fit a time-varying Cox model. All models were adjusted for study-level covariables: sex, age, and study-level clustering. Microsatellite instability status, tumour-sidedness, line of therapy, ECOG performance status, RAS/co-mutation status, and post-progression treatment data were not consistently available across reconstructed IPD and could not be included as covariates (see Limitations).

We corrected for multiple comparisons using a Bonferroni adjustment and considered a P-value < 0.008 as significant. All analyses were conducted using R v4.5.2 and RStudio.

Eighteen RCTs published between 2011 and 2025 met inclusion criteria, comprising predominantly multicentre phase II–III studies evaluating anti-EGFR-, anti-VEGF-, and BRAF inhibitor-containing strategies in mCRC [11, 13, 15, 16, 21–33]. Trials were conducted across Europe, North America, Australia, and multinational cooperative groups. Across studies, 11,931 patients were enrolled. Sample sizes ranged from 96 to 2,326 participants. The largest trial was CALGB/SWOG 80,405, followed by MRC COIN and the pooled analysis of CRYSTAL and OPUS. Molecularly selected BRAF V600E populations were evaluated primarily in BEACON CRC, SWOG S1406, and BREAKWATER. Across trials, the weighted median age approximated 62.4 years and women comprised approximately 39% of participants. The majority of patients (> 85%) had ECOG performance status 0–1. Colon primaries predominated. Among studies reporting metastatic distribution, liver metastases were present in approximately 63% of patients, followed by lung involvement; peritoneal metastases were less common. A summary of the risk of bias assessment is presented in Fig. 2. Overall, most studies were judged as having some methodological concerns, with only five studies achieving an overall low risk of bias. Domains four and five accounted for most concerns, primarily due to unblinded assessment of PFS, and uncertainty regarding whether BRAF-mutant-specific treatment comparison had been prespecified, respectively.

Pooled median OS across monotherapy therapeutic classes in studies evaluating first-line therapy were as follows: for BRAF-directed regimen it was 22.3 months (95% CI: 20.9–29.6). For VEGF-targeted regimens 17.1 months (95% CI 15.2–19.9) and for EGFR-targeted regimens 10.1 months (95% CI: 9.00-11.40).

Across studies evaluating first-line treatment, in 8 studies (n = 746 patients), BRAF inhibitor directed regimens were associated with statistically significant improvement in OS compared with EGFR directed regimens (HR 0.43, 95% CI 0.31–0.60; P < 0.001). Similarly, in 12 studies (n = 648), VEGF inhibitors demonstrated statistically significant improvement in OS compared with EGFR inhibitors (HR 0.56, 95% CI 0.38–0.81; P < 0.001). However, BRAF inhibitor directed regimen showed no statistically significant effect on OS versus VEGF inhibitor directed regiments (HR 0.61, 95% CI 0.31–1.20; P = 0.152) in a clustered model but suggest statistical significance in an unclustered model (P = 0.012). However, unlike other comparisons, the comparison of BRAF-inhibitors versus VEGF-inhibitors did not survive correction for multiple testing (Fig. 3).

KM curves for mCRC patients who received monotherapy

Across studies evaluating first-line treatment, compared to dual VEGF and EGFR inhibition, therapy with BRAF directed regimen (4 studies; n = 797; 507 events) improved OS and the differences were statistically significant (HR 0.55, 95% CI 0.52–0.58; P < 0.001). This effect was also seen in the analysis which incorporated both first- and second-line studies. Although, after subgrouping to first-line studies there was no available data for other comparisons.

Across all studies, compared to BRAF and EGFR inhibition (3 studies; n = 887; 542 events), BRAF directed regimen suggested a benefit with statistically significant difference (HR 0.34, 95% CI 0.28–0.41; P < 0.001). In contrast, EGFR directed regimen versus BRAF plus EGFR therapy did not show a statistically significant difference in OS (9 studies; n = 1,116; 816 events; HR 1.25, 95% CI 0.94–1.68; P = 0.131).

Of note, this indirect comparison does not reflect head-to-head randomized evidence, and the apparent finding should not be interpreted as supporting BRAF directed regimen over established combination regimens. In addition, it is plausible that the analysis incorporating all studies is confounded by the presence of first- and second-line studies.

Regarding pooled median PFS, for BRAF-directed regimens, it was 9.9 months (95% CI 8.6–11.60), for VEGF-targeted regimens, 7.9 months (95% CI 7.3–10.6) and for EGFR-targeted regimens, 5.6 months (95% CI 4.8–7.1).

Across 7 studies, BRAF directed regimen was associated with a statistically significant improvement in PFS compared with EGFR directed regimen (HR 0.24, 95% CI 0.20–0.29; P < 0.001). This effect was also significant in the subgroup analysis limited to first-line studies (HR 0.47, 95% CI 0.42–0.53; P < 0.001). Similarly, VEGF directed regimen was associated with a statistically significant improvement in PFS compared with EGFR directed regimen (HR 0.46, 95% CI 0.33–0.64; P < 0.001) across all studies as well as in the subgroup analysis limited to first-line studies (HR 0.53, 95% CI 0.42–0.68; P < 0.001). There was no statistically significant difference in PFS between BRAF versus VEGF directed regimen (HR 0.68, 95% CI 0.35–1.33; P = 0.265) across all studies (Fig. 3).

Compared to dual VEGF and EGFR inhibition (3 studies; n = 767; 567 events), BRAF-directed regimen suggested a statistically significant improvement in PFS (HR 0.73, 95% CI 0.71–0.74; P < 0.001) across first-line studies. Likely confounded by the mix of first- and second-line studies, in the analysis involving both types of studies, BRAF directed regimen compared to combined BRAF and EGFR inhibition (3 studies) suggested a statistically significant PFS benefit (HR 0.43, 95% CI 0.41–0.47; P < 0.001). In contrast, EGFR-directed regimen versus BRAF + EGFR therapy was not associated with a statistically significant difference in PFS (HR 1.54, 95% CI 0.97–2.45; P = 0.068).

In this reconstructed IPD meta-analysis of eighteen RCTs, we provide a class-level survival comparison of targeted therapeutic strategies in BRAF-mutant mCRC, a biologically aggressive subtype with historically poor outcomes. Across pooled analyses, when compared against each other, a consistent survival gradient emerged: BRAF-directed regimens were associated with the most favourable OS and PFS, VEGF-targeted strategies demonstrated intermediate outcomes, and EGFR directed regimen was associated with the least favourable survival. Hazard-based comparisons confirmed statistically significant differences favouring BRAF-directed therapy over EGFR directed regimen for both endpoints and VEGF-directed therapy over EGFR inhibition for OS. These findings quantitatively define relative therapeutic performance across biologically distinct treatment classes in a molecularly enriched population.

The limited survival observed with EGFR directed regimen is biologically coherent. Constitutive activation of the MAPK pathway in BRAF V600E–mutated tumours renders upstream EGFR blockade insufficient to meaningfully suppress oncogenic signalling [34]. This intrinsic resistance mechanism has been consistently demonstrated in translational and clinical studies and is reflected in our pooled survival estimates [35]. Mechanistic studies have shown that BRAF inhibition in colorectal cancer paradoxically triggers rapid feedback reactivation of EGFR, which in turn reactivates RAS and CRAF-dependent MAPK signalling, a phenomenon far more pronounced in colorectal cancer than in BRAF-mutant melanoma, where BRAF inhibitor monotherapy is far more effective [36, 37]. This EGFR-driven reactivation has also been identified as a recurrent mechanism of acquired resistance in patients treated with RAF-inhibitor based regimens, with sequencing of post-progression tumours revealing KRAS and BRAF amplification and MEK1 mutations that restore MAPK pathway flux [38]. Collectively, these findings explain why regimens combining BRAF and EGFR inhibition — which more durably suppress MAPK signalling than either agent alone — have translated into superior clinical outcomes, as demonstrated in BEACON CRC and BREAKWATER [39]. By contrast, therapies that directly target BRAF-driven signalling demonstrate closer alignment with tumour biology and correspondingly more favourable survival outcomes [40]. Although early phase studies of single-agent BRAF inhibitors in colorectal cancer showed modest durability of response, contemporary BRAF-directed strategies have evolved substantially, often incorporating rational pathway co-inhibition and optimized sequencing, which likely contributes to the improved survival distributions observed in modern datasets [14].

Importantly, the apparent superiority of BRAF directed regimen over BRAF-EGFR combination therapy in our pooled analyses across all studies should not be interpreted as evidence that monotherapy is clinically preferable. This finding is inconsistent with level 1 evidence from the BEACON CRC and BREAKWATER trials, both of which demonstrated superior efficacy with combined pathway inhibition in randomized head-to-head comparisons [15, 16]. The discordance in our analysis is a methodological artifact arising from the structure of indirect cross-trial comparisons: BRAF directed regimen data are derived predominantly from the BREAKWATER trial’s encorafenib–cetuximab doublet arm (which itself includes an anti-EGFR component and was paired with a strong chemotherapy comparator), while BRAF–EGFR combination data are drawn from trials with different patient populations, lines of therapy, and comparator-arm compositions. Hazard ratios estimated across trials are relative to their respective control arms and are therefore not directly comparable. This finding underscores a fundamental limitation of indirect treatment comparisons and should not be used to inform clinical decision-making. Indeed, after subgrouping to first-line studies, there was no available data to evaluate this relationship further.

VEGF-targeted therapy occupied an intermediate position in the survival gradient, with statistically significant differences in OS relative to EGFR inhibition but more modest and less consistent effects on PFS. This dissociation between radiographic progression and OS has been described in prior CRC studies and may reflect effects on tumour vascular normalization, metastatic dissemination, and facilitation of subsequent systemic therapy rather than direct cytotoxic impact [41–43]. However, much of the VEGF literature derives from molecularly unselected populations, and extrapolation to BRAF-mutant disease warrants caution [44]. Nonetheless, our findings support that angiogenesis inhibition continues to confer clinically meaningful survival benefits within this molecular subgroup.

Collectively, these results reinforce the central importance of biologically aligned therapy in BRAF-mutant mCRC. EGFR directed regimen demonstrates limited clinical utility in this context, whereas pathway-directed approaches yield more favourable outcomes. At the same time, our findings illustrate the complexity of synthesizing heterogeneous randomized data across evolving therapeutic eras. Differences in trial design, chemotherapy backbone, prior therapy exposure, and availability of post-progression treatment likely influence absolute survival estimates and may attenuate indirect class comparisons. These considerations are particularly relevant in BRAF-mutant disease, where prognosis is influenced by tumour sidedness, microsatellite instability, and co-mutation status; variables that could not be uniformly adjusted for in the present analysis [45–47].

This study has several notable strengths. Reconstructed IPD permitted consistent time-to-event modelling across trials and enabled direct hazard-based comparisons between therapeutic classes, improving precision relative to aggregate-level meta-analyses. Inclusion of exclusively RCTs enhances internal validity, and the large, pooled sample provides one of the most comprehensive contemporary survival syntheses in this molecularly defined population. However, limitations merit consideration. Reconstructed IPD cannot fully substitute for access to original patient-level datasets. Critically, our adjusted models accounted only for age, sex, and study-level clustering; several clinically important prognostic variables in BRAF-mutant mCRC including microsatellite instability status, tumour sidedness, line of therapy, ECOG performance status, RAS/co-mutation status, and post-progression treatment exposure, were unavailable at the reconstructed IPD level and could not be incorporated into the models. Because these variables are known to independently influence survival in this population and may be unevenly distributed across therapeutic classes and trials, their omission represents a substantial constraint on causal interpretation: the HRs reported here should be understood as adjusted class-level associations rather than causally identified treatment effects. We acknowledge that the survival gradient described in this analysis is derived from indirect, cross-trial comparisons and therefore cannot establish comparative superiority with the same inferential strength as randomized head-to-head evidence. Included trials differed substantially in line of therapy, chemotherapy backbone, treatment era, patient selection criteria, comparator-arm composition, and availability of post-progression therapies all of which may confound class-level hazard estimates. Given this incomplete confounder adjustment, residual confounding cannot be excluded as a contributor to the observed between-class differences. Accordingly, the observed survival gradient should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating and descriptive of relative therapeutic performance across trials, rather than as definitive evidence of causal superiority of one class over another.

An additional source of heterogeneity is that several older included trials (e.g., MRC COIN, NORDIC-VII, CRYSTAL/OPUS) enrolled molecularly unselected populations, with BRAF-mutant subgroups identified through post-hoc analyses. These subgroups were often small, and the trials were not powered to detect treatment effects within the BRAF-mutant subset. In contrast, BEACON CRC and BREAKWATER prospectively enrolled BRAF V600E–mutant patients. This difference in molecular enrichment strategy may influence the precision and generalizability of survival estimates across therapeutic classes.

This meta-analysis characterizes relative survival patterns across targeted therapeutic classes in BRAF-mutant mCRC. While BRAF-directed strategies were associated with the most favourable survival profiles in pooled analyses, these findings are derived from indirect cross-trial comparisons and should be interpreted as complementary to, rather than a substitute for, randomized head-to-head evidence.

Current level 1 evidence from the BEACON CRC and BREAKWATER trials supports encorafenib-based combination therapy (with cetuximab ± chemotherapy) as the standard of care for BRAF V600E–mutant mCRC. The indirect comparisons presented herein are exploratory and hypothesis-generating and do not supersede direct randomized evidence. Continued prospective, biomarker-stratified investigation will be essential to refine optimal sequencing and further improve outcomes in this high-risk population.
